    def plot_current_sharing(
    result: "FieldResult",
    world: "World | None" = None,
    *,
    by: Literal["electrode", "cluster"] = "electrode",
    top_n: int = 15,
    frequency_index: int = 0,
    figsize: tuple[float, float] = (8.0, 5.0),
    title: str | None = None,
):
    """Bar chart of the ``top_n`` current contributors.

    Renders ``|I|`` (in A) for either every electrode or every
    galvanic cluster, sorted descending. The default ``by =
    "electrode"`` is the default — *which physical electrode
    actually carries the test current?* The companion option
    ``by = "cluster"`` aggregates over each cluster.

    Parameters
    ----------
    result
        Solver output.
    world
        Optional companion world. Forwarded to
        :func:`electrode_current_table` for the kind / depth
        annotations; ignored otherwise.
    by
        ``"electrode"`` (default) or ``"cluster"``.
    top_n
        Maximum number of bars to render. Smaller contributors are
        truncated. Pass ``0`` to render all.
    frequency_index
        Index into :attr:`FieldResult.frequencies`.
    figsize
        Matplotlib figure size in inches.
    title
        Optional title override.

    Returns
    -------
    matplotlib.figure.Figure

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``by`` is neither ``"electrode"`` nor ``"cluster"``.
    """
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    if by == "electrode":
        df = electrode_current_table(
            result, world=world, frequency_index=frequency_index
        )
        labels = df["name"].tolist()
        magnitudes = df["abs_I"].to_numpy()
        ylabel = "|I| in A (per electrode)"
    elif by == "cluster":
        df = cluster_current_balance(result, frequency_index=frequency_index)
        labels = df["cluster_root"].tolist()
        magnitudes = df["abs_sum_I"].to_numpy()
        ylabel = "|ΣI| in A (per cluster)"
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"by must be 'electrode' or 'cluster', got {by!r}.")

    if top_n and top_n > 0:
        labels = labels[:top_n]
        magnitudes = magnitudes[:top_n]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    ax.bar(range(len(labels)), magnitudes, color="C0")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(labels)))
    ax.set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=45, ha="right")
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax.grid(True, axis="y", alpha=0.3)

    if title is None:
        f_hz = result.frequencies[frequency_index]
        suffix = f"top {top_n}" if (top_n and top_n > 0) else "all"
        title = f"Current sharing by {by} — {suffix}, f = {f_hz:g} Hz"
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

    split_factor ¶

    split_factor(result: 'FieldResult', world: 'World', *, source_name: str | None = None, frequency_index: int = 0) -> complex

    Split factor \(s = I_{c_\text{src}} / I_\text{src}\).

    Computes the galvanic split factor of a current source: the fraction of the injected current that leaves the source cluster through the soil rather than through any metallic parallel path (PEN trunk, parallel measurement lead, cable shield).

    Mathematically

    \[ s \;=\; \frac{\sum_{e \in c_\text{src}} I_e}{I_\text{src}}, \]

    with \(c_\text{src}\) the galvanic cluster of the source's attached_to electrode and \(I_\text{src}\) the complex phasor of the source. By construction:

    • For a stand-alone source on an electrode without metallic parallel paths, KCL forces \(s = 1 + 0\,j\). The injected current leaves the cluster entirely through the soil.
    • For a source whose cluster is connected to another grounding cluster (e.g. the auxiliary electrode of a fall-of-potential measurement) by a metallic conductor, \(s < 1\). The smaller the conductor's series impedance, the smaller \(s\).
    • The complex argument \(\arg s\) reveals the inductive content of the parallel path — a Carson- or Sommerfeld- corrected lead at frequency >0 produces an imaginary share.
    • For a source returning through remote earth it links the input impedance and the cluster impedance of the feeding cluster, \(Z_\text{in} = s\,Z_c\) (review pass 10, 10.18).

    The denominator \(I_\text{src}\) is the source current of the solve, read from the snapshot FieldResult.sources when the result carries one (since review pass 10); otherwise from the world's source. For a voltage source it is the solved source current (since 2026.11).

    Not to be confused with the Reduktionsfaktor

    In the German EVU / Schirmtechnik literature (Oeding & Oswald 2016), the Reduktionsfaktor refers to the transformatorische / inductive coupling correction between a current-carrying conductor and a parallel grounding / shield conductor. That quantity is angle-dependent: it vanishes when the two conductors are perpendicular (no flux linkage) but is large for collinear runs.

    The split factor implemented here is purely galvanic — the resistive division of current across parallel paths. It is present whenever there are multiple parallel paths, regardless of their geometric orientation.

    Solver output.

    Index into FieldResult.frequencies. Default 0.

    def split_factor(
    result: "FieldResult",
    world: "World",
    *,
    source_name: str | None = None,
    frequency_index: int = 0,
) -> complex:
    """Split factor :math:`s = I_{c_\\text{src}} / I_\\text{src}`.

    Computes the **galvanic split factor** of a current source:
    the fraction of the injected current that leaves the source
    cluster through the **soil** rather than through any metallic
    parallel path (PEN trunk, parallel measurement lead, cable
    shield).

    Mathematically

    .. math::

        s \\;=\\; \\frac{\\sum_{e \\in c_\\text{src}} I_e}{I_\\text{src}},

    with :math:`c_\\text{src}` the galvanic cluster of the source's
    ``attached_to`` electrode and :math:`I_\\text{src}` the complex
    phasor of the source. By construction:

    * For a stand-alone source on an electrode without metallic
      parallel paths, KCL forces :math:`s = 1 + 0\\,j`. The
      injected current leaves the cluster entirely through the
      soil.
    * For a source whose cluster is connected to *another*
      grounding cluster (e.g. the auxiliary electrode of a
      fall-of-potential measurement) by a metallic conductor,
      :math:`s < 1`. The smaller the conductor's series
      impedance, the smaller :math:`s`.
    * The complex argument :math:`\\arg s` reveals the inductive
      content of the parallel path — a Carson- or Sommerfeld-
      corrected lead at frequency >0 produces an imaginary share.
    * For a source returning through remote earth it links the input
      impedance and the cluster impedance of the feeding cluster,
      :math:`Z_\\text{in} = s\\,Z_c` (review pass 10, 10.18).

    The denominator :math:`I_\\text{src}` is the source current of the
    solve, read from the snapshot :attr:`FieldResult.sources` when the
    result carries one (since review pass 10); otherwise from the
    world's source. For a voltage source it is the solved source current
    (since 2026.11).

    Not to be confused with the *Reduktionsfaktor*
    -----------------------------------------------
    In the German EVU / Schirmtechnik literature (Oeding & Oswald
    2016), the *Reduktionsfaktor* refers to the **transformatorische
    / inductive coupling correction** between a current-carrying
    conductor and a parallel grounding / shield conductor. That
    quantity is angle-dependent: it vanishes when the two conductors
    are perpendicular (no flux linkage) but is large for collinear
    runs.

    The split factor implemented here is **purely galvanic** — the
    resistive division of current across parallel paths. It is
    present whenever there are multiple parallel paths, regardless
    of their geometric orientation.

    Parameters
    ----------
    result
        Solver output.
    world
        Companion world used to resolve the source object.
    source_name
        Optional name of the current source. ``None`` (default)
        picks the unique current source; raises if the world
        contains more than one.
    frequency_index
        Index into :attr:`FieldResult.frequencies`. Default 0.

    Returns
    -------
    complex
        Phasor :math:`s(f)` (dimensionless).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the world has no current source, multiple current
        sources without explicit ``source_name``, or the source
        has zero magnitude.
    KeyError
        If ``source_name`` does not exist among current sources,
        or the source's ``attached_to`` electrode is unknown to
        the result.
    """
    source = _resolve_source(world, source_name)
    I_src = _solved_source_current(result, source, frequency_index)
    if abs(I_src) == 0.0:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Source '{source.name}' has zero magnitude — split factor is undefined."
        )

    attached = source.attached_to
    members = result.clusters.get(attached, [attached])
    if not members:
        raise KeyError(
            f"Source '{source.name}' is attached to '{attached}', "
            "which has no cluster entry in the result."
        )

    sum_I = 0.0 + 0j
    for m in members:
        if m in result.electrode_currents:
            sum_I += complex(result.electrode_currents[m][frequency_index])
    return sum_I / I_src

    Sweeps and convergence studies¶

    sweep ¶

    Cartesian-product parameter sweeps for parameter axis studies.

    This module turns the typical study axes — soil resistivity \(\rho_1\) / \(\rho_2\), layer thickness \(h_1\), electrode geometry, frequency — into a single tabular response that is cheap to plot and easy to feed into vector-fitting, \(\rho\)-\(f\) regression, or downstream groundinsight.

    API surface

    sweep() Walk the Cartesian product of an arbitrary number of named axes, build a fresh World (and optionally a fresh Engine) per combination, solve, and extract a scalar response per frequency. Returns a long-format pandas.DataFrame with one row per (axis values × frequency). plot_sweep_lines() Line plot of one response column against a chosen axis, optionally with one curve per value of a second axis. plot_sweep_heatmap() Pivot-table heatmap of one response column over a (x_axis, y_axis) pair (e.g. \(\rho_1\) vs. \(h_1\)).

    Mathematical / physical content

    The default response extractor reports one impedance per frequency, selected by quantity (review pass 10, 10.18):

    • "input" (default) — the input (driving-point) impedance \(Z_\text{in} = (\varphi_a - \varphi_r) / I_s\) of the current source: what a measurement instrument or a fault sees at the feeding point (FieldResult.input_impedance());
    • "cluster" — the cluster impedance \(Z_c = \varphi_c / \sum_{e \in c} I_e\) of the source's galvanic cluster over its own soil leakage (the default up to v0.15.0);
    • "electrode" — \(\varphi_e / I_e\) of the feeding electrode alone.

    As soon as conductors (PEN, shields, leads) carry part of the injected current away, the cluster impedance describes only the local electrode: for a station with three houses on a PEN it is 1.79 times the input impedance (1.26 times with one house, 3.09 times with eight; review pass 10). The response is the engineering \(Z(\rho_1, h_1, f)\) curve that groundfield.postprocess.rho_f_standard and groundfield.postprocess.vector_fitting consume.

    Validity envelope
    • Frequency: quasi-static envelope \(f \le 1\,\mathrm{kHz}\).
    • Linearity: the sweep does not interpolate between samples — for a smooth \(Z(\rho, f)\) surface, hand the resulting DataFrame to fit_rho_f_standard() / fit_to_sympy_standard().
    • Cost: every Cartesian combination triggers one full Engine.solve(). For 50 ρ-values × 10 h-values × 1 frequency list with N segments each, expect 500 dense system solves; budget accordingly with expected_segments().
    • Parallelism: the combinations are independent, so sweep(..., n_jobs=k) solves them in k worker processes (review pass 10, 10.64). The dense LU factorisation is only 0.2–1.5 % of a solve (kernel assembly dominates), so a multi-threaded BLAS does not parallelise a solve; separate processes do (measured 1.98× on 2 workers for a 20-house world). Workers run their BLAS on one thread; the result is bit-identical to the serial run when the calling process also runs a single-threaded BLAS (results differ at the 1e-15 level between 1 and 2 BLAS threads).

    def plot_sweep_heatmap(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    x: str,
    y: str,
    response: str = "abs_Z",
    frequency_Hz: float | None = None,
    agg: str = "mean",
    cmap: str = "viridis",
    figsize: tuple[float, float] = (7.5, 5.5),
    title: str | None = None,
):
    """Heatmap of ``response`` over the ``(x, y)`` axis pair.

    Pivot-tables ``df`` by ``y`` (rows) and ``x`` (columns),
    aggregating ``response`` with the chosen ``agg`` (default
    ``"mean"`` — useful when the sweep contains additional axes
    that should collapse). Selects a single frequency slice
    when ``frequency_Hz`` is given.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df
        Long-format DataFrame from :func:`sweep`.
    x, y
        Column names for the heatmap axes. Both must be numeric.
    response
        Column to colour-code. Default ``"abs_Z"``.
    frequency_Hz
        If given and the DataFrame has a ``frequency_Hz`` column,
        keep only rows that match this frequency. Raises if no
        rows match.
    agg
        Aggregation passed to :meth:`pd.DataFrame.pivot_table`.
        Default ``"mean"``.
    cmap, figsize, title
        Standard matplotlib options.

    Returns
    -------
    matplotlib.figure.Figure

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If ``x``, ``y`` or ``response`` is not a column of ``df``.
    ValueError
        If ``frequency_Hz`` is given and no row matches it.
    """
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    for col in (x, y, response):
        if col not in df.columns:
            raise KeyError(f"column '{col}' not in DataFrame; have: {list(df.columns)}")

    sub = df
    if frequency_Hz is not None and "frequency_Hz" in df.columns:
        sub = df[df["frequency_Hz"] == frequency_Hz]
        if sub.empty:
            raise ValueError(
                f"No rows match frequency_Hz={frequency_Hz}; "
                f"available: {sorted(df['frequency_Hz'].unique())}"
            )

    pivot = sub.pivot_table(index=y, columns=x, values=response, aggfunc=agg)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    im = ax.imshow(
        pivot.values,
        origin="lower",
        aspect="auto",
        extent=(
            float(pivot.columns.min()),
            float(pivot.columns.max()),
            float(pivot.index.min()),
            float(pivot.index.max()),
        ),
        cmap=cmap,
        interpolation="nearest",
    )
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label=response)
    ax.set_xlabel(x)
    ax.set_ylabel(y)
    if title is None:
        title = f"{response}({x}, {y})"
        if frequency_Hz is not None:
            title += f"  @ f = {frequency_Hz:g} Hz"
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

    def plot_sweep_lines(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    x: str,
    y: str = "abs_Z",
    color: str | None = None,
    figsize: tuple[float, float] = (8.0, 5.0),
    log_x: bool = False,
    log_y: bool = False,
    title: str | None = None,
):
    """Line plot of ``y`` versus ``x``, one curve per ``color`` value.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df
        Long-format DataFrame as produced by :func:`sweep`.
    x
        Column name to use on the x-axis.
    y
        Column name of the response. Default ``"abs_Z"``.
    color
        Optional second column name; one line per distinct value
        is drawn. ``None`` (default) collapses to a single line.
    figsize, log_x, log_y, title
        Standard matplotlib options.

    Returns
    -------
    matplotlib.figure.Figure

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If ``x``, ``y`` or ``color`` is not a column of ``df``.
    """
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    if x not in df.columns:
        raise KeyError(f"column '{x}' not in DataFrame; have: {list(df.columns)}")
    if y not in df.columns:
        raise KeyError(f"column '{y}' not in DataFrame; have: {list(df.columns)}")

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    if color is None:
        sub = df.sort_values(x)
        ax.plot(sub[x], sub[y], marker="o")
    else:
        if color not in df.columns:
            raise KeyError(
                f"color column '{color}' not in DataFrame; have: {list(df.columns)}"
            )
        for val, sub in df.groupby(color):
            sub = sub.sort_values(x)
            ax.plot(sub[x], sub[y], marker="o", label=f"{color} = {val}")
        ax.legend()

    if log_x:
        ax.set_xscale("log")
    if log_y:
        ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel(x)
    ax.set_ylabel(y)
    ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.3)
    if title is None:
        title = f"{y} vs. {x}" + (f"  (color: {color})" if color else "")
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

    sweep ¶

    sweep(world_factory: Callable[..., 'World'], engine: 'Engine | Callable[..., Engine]', *, axes: dict[str, Sequence[Any]], response: Callable[['FieldResult', 'World', int], dict[str, float]] | None = None, quantity: Quantity = 'input', source: str | None = None, n_jobs: int = 1) -> pd.DataFrame

    Cartesian-product parameter sweep across user-defined axes.

    For every combination (a_1 = v_1, a_2 = v_2, ...) in the Cartesian product of axes, the function

    1. builds a fresh world via world_factory(**combination),
    2. resolves the engine — either the static Engine passed in or a per-combination engine via engine(**combination) if a callable is given,
    3. solves with World.solve(),
    4. iterates over every frequency in FieldResult.frequencies and extracts a row via response(result, world, frequency_index).

    The axis values and frequency_Hz are added to every row automatically.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    world_factory Callable[..., 'World']

    Callable that builds a fresh World from the per-combination kwargs. Must return a fully populated world (soil, electrodes, sources, optional conductors).

    		 required
    engine 'Engine | Callable[..., Engine]'

    Either a static Engine (reused for every combination) or a callable engine(**combination) -> Engine (rebuilt per combination — useful when the segment length depends on the geometry).

    		 required
    axes dict[str, Sequence[Any]]

    Mapping axis_name -> Sequence of values. Must contain at least one axis. Empty sequences raise immediately.

    		 required
    response Callable[['FieldResult', 'World', int], dict[str, float]] | None

    Optional response extractor. Receives (result, world, frequency_index) and must return a dict[str, float|complex]. Defaults to the impedance selected by quantity with the columns U_E_re, U_E_im, abs_U_E, I_re, I_im, abs_I, Z_re, Z_im, abs_Z, arg_Z_deg (see the module docstring).

    		 None
    quantity Quantity

    Impedance of the default response: "input" (default since review pass 10, 10.18) — the driving-point impedance of the source; "cluster" — the source cluster's potential over its own leakage (the v0.15.0 default); "electrode" — the feeding electrode's own U/I. Only with the default response.

    		 'input'
    source str | None

    Name of the current source the default response refers to; may be omitted when the world has exactly one current source (with several, v0.15.0 silently used the first one; now it raises).

    		 None
    n_jobs int

    Number of worker processes (default 1: serial, in this process). -1 uses every logical CPU. With n_jobs > 1 the combinations are solved in a process pool (spawn start method, BLAS pinned to one thread per worker); rows keep the order of the serial run and warnings raised in the workers are re-issued here. world_factory, engine and response must then be picklable: module-level functions or an Engine, not lambdas or functions defined in a notebook (put those into a small .py module).

    		 1

    Returns:

    Type Description
    DataFrame

    Long-format. Columns are the axis names, frequency_Hz, and every key returned by response. One row per Cartesian-product point per frequency. With the default response, df.attrs["impedance_quantity"] records quantity.

    Raises:

    Type Description
    ValueError

    If axes is empty or any axis is empty, quantity is unknown, quantity / source are combined with a custom response, the default response finds several current sources and source is omitted, or n_jobs is 0 or below -1.
    TypeError

    With n_jobs > 1, if a callable cannot be sent to the worker processes.
    Notes

    With n_jobs > 1 the result is bit-identical to n_jobs=1 when the calling process runs a single-threaded BLAS as well (OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1); otherwise the two agree to round-off. Process start-up costs about a second per worker, so parallel runs pay off for solves of a second or more.

    """Cartesian-product parameter sweep across user-defined axes.

    For every combination ``(a_1 = v_1, a_2 = v_2, ...)`` in the

    1. builds a fresh world via ``world_factory(**combination)``,

    4. iterates over every frequency in
       :attr:`FieldResult.frequencies` and extracts a row via
       ``response(result, world, frequency_index)``.

    The axis values and ``frequency_Hz`` are added to every row
    automatically.

    Parameters
    ----------
    world_factory
        Callable that builds a fresh :class:`World` from the
        per-combination kwargs. Must return a fully populated
        world (soil, electrodes, sources, optional conductors).
    engine
        Either a static :class:`Engine` (reused for every
        combination) or a callable
        ``engine(**combination) -> Engine`` (rebuilt per
        combination — useful when the segment length depends on
        the geometry).
    axes
        Mapping ``axis_name -> Sequence`` of values. Must contain
        at least one axis. Empty sequences raise immediately.
    response
        Optional response extractor. Receives
        ``(result, world, frequency_index)`` and must return a
        ``dict[str, float|complex]``. Defaults to the impedance
        selected by ``quantity`` with the columns ``U_E_re``,
        ``U_E_im``, ``abs_U_E``, ``I_re``, ``I_im``, ``abs_I``,
        ``Z_re``, ``Z_im``, ``abs_Z``, ``arg_Z_deg`` (see the module
        docstring).
    quantity
        Impedance of the default response: ``"input"`` (default since
        review pass 10, 10.18) — the driving-point impedance of the
        source; ``"cluster"`` — the source cluster's potential over its
        own leakage (the v0.15.0 default); ``"electrode"`` — the feeding
        electrode's own U/I. Only with the default response.
    source
        Name of the current source the default response refers to; may
        be omitted when the world has exactly one current source (with
        several, v0.15.0 silently used the first one; now it raises).
    n_jobs
        Number of worker processes (default 1: serial, in this process).
        ``-1`` uses every logical CPU. With ``n_jobs > 1`` the
        combinations are solved in a process pool (``spawn`` start
        method, BLAS pinned to one thread per worker); rows keep the
        order of the serial run and warnings raised in the workers are
        re-issued here. ``world_factory``, ``engine`` and ``response``
        must then be picklable: module-level functions or an
        :class:`Engine`, not lambdas or functions defined in a notebook
        (put those into a small ``.py`` module).

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        Long-format. Columns are the axis names, ``frequency_Hz``,
        and every key returned by ``response``. One row per
        Cartesian-product point per frequency. With the default
        response, ``df.attrs["impedance_quantity"]`` records
        ``quantity``.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``axes`` is empty or any axis is empty, ``quantity`` is
        unknown, ``quantity`` / ``source`` are combined with a custom
        ``response``, the default response finds several current
        sources and ``source`` is omitted, or ``n_jobs`` is 0 or below -1.
    TypeError
        With ``n_jobs > 1``, if a callable cannot be sent to the worker
        processes.

    Notes
    -----
    With ``n_jobs > 1`` the result is bit-identical to ``n_jobs=1``
    when the calling process runs a single-threaded BLAS as well
    (``OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1``); otherwise the two agree to round-off.
    Process start-up costs about a second per worker, so parallel runs
    pay off for solves of a second or more.
    """
    from groundfield.solver.engine import Engine

    if not axes:
        raise ValueError("axes must contain at least one axis.")
    for name, values in axes.items():
        if len(list(values)) == 0:
            raise ValueError(f"axis '{name}' is empty.")

    default = response is None
    response = _resolve_response(response, quantity, source, "sweep")
    if isinstance(n_jobs, bool) or not isinstance(n_jobs, int):
        raise ValueError(f"n_jobs must be an integer, got {n_jobs!r}.")
    if n_jobs == -1:
        n_jobs = os.cpu_count() or 1
    if n_jobs < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"n_jobs must be >= 1 or -1, got {n_jobs}.")

    keys = list(axes.keys())
    values_list = [list(axes[k]) for k in keys]
    combos = [dict(zip(keys, c, strict=True)) for c in itertools.product(*values_list)]

    rows: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    if n_jobs == 1 or len(combos) == 1:
        for params in combos:
            world = world_factory(**params)
            eng = engine if isinstance(engine, Engine) else engine(**params)
            result = eng.solve(world)
            for f_idx, f_hz in enumerate(result.frequencies):
                row = dict(params)
                row["frequency_Hz"] = float(f_hz)
                row.update(response(result, world, f_idx))
                rows.append(row)
    else:
        rows = _parallel_rows(world_factory, engine, response, combos, n_jobs)
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    if default:
        df.attrs["impedance_quantity"] = quantity
    return df

    convergence ¶

    Convergence study over the engine's segment_length.

    The PDE / field model in groundfield is a reference computation (see CLAUDE.md); to honour that role every non-trivial result should be backed up by a refinement study. This module turns the canonical "halve the segment length, watch what happens" experiment into one function call.

    Mathematical / physical content

    The image-family discretiser splits each electrode into segments of length \(\Delta s\). As \(\Delta s \to 0\) the multi-port grounding matrix approaches the continuous integral operator and the cluster impedance \(Z_c\) converges to the PDE-grade reference. The convergence is monotone in \(\Delta s\) for the average-potential method (cf. Sunde 1968; Tagg 1964). A practical refinement plot therefore answers two questions at once:

    • "Has my chosen \(\Delta s\) already converged within X %?" — the curve flattens out.
    • "What is the asymptotic (PDE-grade) value?" — extrapolation / Richardson if needed.
    Validity envelope
    • Frequency: quasi-static envelope \(f \le 1\,\mathrm{kHz}\).
    • Backends: any image-family solver (image / image_2layer / image_nlayer / mom / mom_sommerfeld / cim / bem). FEM is supported but its mesh is generated independently — the segment_length knob does not directly control its accuracy.
    • The function copies the engine per step (the original engine is not mutated) without the validating Engine.model_copy(), whose warning capture resets every module's "shown once" registry: a warning that a plain loop over the same engines shows once was shown once per step (audit round 2, A2S-08). The segment lengths are validated here instead.

    def convergence_study(
    world: "World",
    engine: "Engine",
    *,
    segment_lengths: Sequence[float],
    response: Callable[["FieldResult", "World", int], dict[str, float]] | None = None,
    quantity: Quantity = "input",
    source: str | None = None,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Solve the same world repeatedly with refining ``segment_length``.

    For every :math:`\\Delta s_k` in ``segment_lengths`` the
    function builds a clone of the engine (only ``segment_length``
    differs), solves the world, and extracts a scalar response
    per frequency. The returned DataFrame is sorted **descending**
    in ``segment_length_m`` so finer resolutions land on the right
    in the default plot.

    Parameters
    ----------
    world
        World to solve. **Not modified.**
    engine
        Base engine. Cloned per refinement step via
        an internal copy per step; the original is left untouched.
    segment_lengths
        Sequence of segment lengths in metres. Must be strictly
        positive and contain at least two distinct values.
    response
        Optional response extractor ``(result, world,
        frequency_index) -> dict``. Defaults to the impedance response
        of :func:`groundfield.postprocess.sweep.sweep`.
    quantity
        Impedance of the default response: ``"input"`` (default since
        review pass 10, 10.18; the driving-point impedance of the
        source), ``"cluster"`` (the v0.15.0 default) or ``"electrode"``.
        See :func:`groundfield.postprocess.sweep.sweep`.
    source
        Current source of the default response; may be omitted with a
        single current source.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        Long-format. Columns ``segment_length_m``,
        ``frequency_Hz``, ``n_segments`` and every key of the
        response (e.g. ``Z_re``, ``Z_im``, ``abs_Z``,
        ``arg_Z_deg``, ``U_E_re``, ...). With the default response
        ``df.attrs["impedance_quantity"]`` records ``quantity``.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``segment_lengths`` is empty, contains non-positive
        values, or has fewer than two distinct values (a
        convergence study below two refinement steps is
        meaningless); for an unknown ``quantity``.
    """
    ds_list = [float(ds) for ds in segment_lengths]
    if len(ds_list) < 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"segment_lengths must contain at least 2 values, got {len(ds_list)}."
        )
    if any(not (ds > 0 and math.isfinite(ds)) for ds in ds_list):
        raise ValueError(
            f"segment_lengths must be finite and strictly positive, got {ds_list}."
        )
    if len(set(ds_list)) < 2:
        raise ValueError("segment_lengths must contain at least 2 distinct values.")

    default = response is None
    response = _resolve_response(response, quantity, source, "convergence_study")

    rows: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for ds in ds_list:
        # Not the validating model_copy (A2S-08, see the module docstring);
        # ds is validated above.
        eng = engine._with(segment_length=ds)
        result = world.solve(eng)
        n_seg = len(result.point_sources)
        for f_idx, f_hz in enumerate(result.frequencies):
            row: dict[str, Any] = {
                "segment_length_m": ds,
                "frequency_Hz": float(f_hz),
                "n_segments": n_seg,
            }
            row.update(response(result, world, f_idx))
            rows.append(row)
    df = (
        pd.DataFrame(rows)
        .sort_values(["frequency_Hz", "segment_length_m"], ascending=[True, False])
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )
    if default:
        df.attrs["impedance_quantity"] = quantity
    return df

    def plot_convergence(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    response: str = "abs_Z",
    reference: float | None = None,
    figsize: tuple[float, float] = (7.5, 4.5),
    title: str | None = None,
):
    """Plot ``response`` versus ``segment_length`` (one line per frequency).

    The x-axis is logarithmic and **inverted** so finer
    resolutions sit on the right (the convergence "asymptote
    direction"). When the DataFrame contains a single frequency
    only, the legend is suppressed.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df
        DataFrame returned by :func:`convergence_study`.
    response
        Column name to plot. Default ``"abs_Z"``.
    reference
        Optional asymptotic value to draw as a horizontal dashed
        reference line — useful when an analytical reference
        (Sunde, Dwight, IEEE Std 80) is known.
    figsize, title
        Standard matplotlib options.

    Returns
    -------
    matplotlib.figure.Figure

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If ``df`` has no column ``response`` or no ``segment_length_m``
        column.
    """
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    if response not in df.columns:
        raise KeyError(
            f"column '{response}' not in DataFrame; have: {list(df.columns)}"
        )
    if "segment_length_m" not in df.columns:
        raise KeyError(
            "DataFrame must have a 'segment_length_m' column "
            "(produced by convergence_study)."
        )

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    if "frequency_Hz" in df.columns and df["frequency_Hz"].nunique() > 1:
        for f_hz, sub in df.groupby("frequency_Hz"):
            sub = sub.sort_values("segment_length_m", ascending=False)
            ax.plot(
                sub["segment_length_m"],
                sub[response],
                marker="o",
                label=f"f = {f_hz:g} Hz",
            )
        ax.legend()
    else:
        sub = df.sort_values("segment_length_m", ascending=False)
        ax.plot(sub["segment_length_m"], sub[response], marker="o")

    if reference is not None:
        ax.axhline(
            float(reference),
            ls="--",
            color="k",
            alpha=0.6,
            label=f"reference = {reference:g}",
        )
        # Re-render legend so the reference line appears even in
        # the single-frequency case.
        ax.legend()

    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.invert_xaxis()  # finer ds (smaller value) on the right
    ax.set_xlabel("segment_length in m")
    ax.set_ylabel(response)
    ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.3)
    if title is None:
        title = f"Convergence of {response} vs. segment_length"
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

    Vector fitting¶

    vector_fitting ¶

    Vector fitting and SymPy export for the rho-f reduced model.

    This module turns a frequency response computed by groundfield into a closed-form rational impedance expression that groundinsight can consume as BusType.impedance_formula. It is the bridge between the field-grade reference computation (groundfield) and the reduced equivalent-network model (groundinsight).

    Mathematical background

    For a passive, linear, time-invariant grounding cluster, the driving-point impedance \(Z(s)\) at the feed-in electrode is a rational function of the Laplace variable \(s = j\omega\). Under the \(f \le 1\,\mathrm{kHz}\) assumption the function is well approximated by a low-order partial-fraction expansion

    \[ Z(s) \;\approx\; R_\infty \;+\; s\,L_\infty \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{N_p}\,\frac{r_k}{s - p_k}, \]

    with poles \(p_k\) on the negative real axis (damped RC modes) and residues \(r_k\). Complex-conjugate pole pairs are admissible too — they produce damped resonant LC-like behaviour. The fit is constructed by the Vector Fitting algorithm of Gustavsen & Semlyen 1999, which iterates pole locations to a stable solution and is the de-facto standard for transmission-line and grounding modelling.

    Implementation

    This module implements a clean, dependency-free version of vector fitting in NumPy:

    1. Initial pole guess: linearly spaced on the negative real axis between the smallest and largest sampled frequencies.
    2. Pole relocation via Sanathanan-Koerner-style least squares with a shared denominator (the canonical Gustavsen iteration).
    3. Residue solve given the converged poles.
    4. Stability enforcement: any pole ending up in the right half plane is reflected.

    The exported SymPy expression follows the groundinsight.BusType.impedance_formula convention: a single free symbol s and arbitrary numeric constants.

    References
    • Gustavsen, B. & Semlyen, A. (1999). Rational approximation of frequency domain responses by Vector Fitting. IEEE Trans. Power Delivery 14(3), 1052–1061.
    • Gustavsen, B. (2006). Improving the pole relocating properties of vector fitting. IEEE Trans. Power Delivery 21(3), 1587–1592.

    def as_dict(self) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Strict-JSON summary; the ``metadata["passivity"]`` block of an export.

    Keys: ``passed``, ``min_re_Z_Ohm`` (``None`` when not finite),
    ``f_at_min_Hz``, ``rho_at_min_Ohm_m``, ``f_checked_Hz``
    (``[0, f_max]``), ``rho_checked_Ohm_m`` (``[min, max]`` or
    ``None``) and ``n_points``.
    """
    finite = math.isfinite(self.min_re_Z)
    return {
        "passed": bool(self.passed),
        "min_re_Z_Ohm": float(self.min_re_Z) if finite else None,
        "f_at_min_Hz": float(self.f_at_min),
        "rho_at_min_Ohm_m": (
            None if self.rho_at_min is None else float(self.rho_at_min)
        ),
        "f_checked_Hz": [0.0, float(self.f_max)],
        "rho_checked_Ohm_m": (
            None if self.rho_range is None else [float(x) for x in self.rho_range]
        ),
        "n_points": int(self.n_points),
    }

    VectorFitConvergenceWarning ¶

    Bases: UserWarning

    The pole-relocation loop did not converge.

    Emitted when the relative pole displacement of the last relocation step is still above 1 % after n_iter iterations (audit 2026-07-08, WP-B4 — the historic implementation ran a fixed number of blind iterations with no convergence check). Inspect VectorFitResult.pole_shift / n_iter_used and consider more iterations, a different n_poles, or weighting="inverse_magnitude" for wide-dynamic-range data.

    VectorFitQualityWarning ¶

    Bases: UserWarning

    The vector fit is poor, or a sample had to be corrected.

    Emitted (review pass 10, 10.41) when the relative rms error rms_error / mean|Z| exceeds rms_tol (default 1 %), and when the imaginary part of a 0 Hz sample exceeds 0.1 % of its magnitude (it is discarded: a rational model with real coefficients is real at \(s = 0\)). Inspect VectorFitResult.rms_relative; try other n_poles, more samples, or weighting="inverse_magnitude".

    def evaluate(self, frequencies: Sequence[float]) -> np.ndarray:
    """Evaluate the fitted $Z(s)$ at arbitrary frequencies."""
    s = 2j * math.pi * np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float)
    Z = np.full_like(s, self.R_inf, dtype=complex)
    Z = Z + self.L_inf * s
    for p, r in zip(self.poles, self.residues, strict=True):
        Z = Z + r / (s - p)
    return Z

    VectorFitUnderdeterminedWarning ¶

    Bases: UserWarning

    Vector fit is under- or exactly-determined.

    A vector fit with n_poles poles has 2 * n_poles + extras real unknowns (residues plus optional R_inf / L_inf); the real-imag stacking of an input of length N gives 2 N equations. n_poles >= N therefore leads to an under- or exactly-determined least-squares problem. The fit can succeed numerically but is effectively an identity interpolation that carries no information beyond the input samples.

    A dedicated warning category lets users opt into / out of the diagnostic with warnings.simplefilter("once", VectorFitUnderdeterminedWarning).

    check_passivity ¶

    check_passivity(fit, f_max: float | None = None, *, n: int = 2001, rho_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None) -> PassivityReport

    Check \(\Re Z(j 2\pi f) \ge 0\) of a fitted rho-f model on a band.

    A grounding impedance is the driving-point impedance of a passive one-port, so its real part is non-negative at every frequency,

    \[ \operatorname{Re} Z(j\,2\pi f) \;\ge\; 0 \qquad (f \ge 0). \]

    A rational fit can violate this between or beyond its samples: review pass 10 found a 4-pole fit of passive data (rms 4.4 mΩ, no warning) with \(\Re Z = -0.019\,\Omega\) at 5.5 Hz, between the 0 Hz and 50 Hz samples (10.40 / 10.41). This is the one passivity check of the package: the groundinsight exporter runs the same implementation on the formula it writes.

The grid also holds 3 n // 10 logarithmically spaced points from \(10^{-6} f_\max\), the samples and the midpoints between them, and 161 points within eight half-widths \(|\Re p|\) of every pole frequency \(|\Im p|/2\pi\), which resolve resonances narrower than any fixed grid.     def check_passivity(
    fit,
    f_max: float | None = None,
    *,
    n: int = 2001,
    rho_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
) -> PassivityReport:
    """Check :math:`\\Re Z(j 2\\pi f) \\ge 0` of a fitted rho-f model on a band.

    A grounding impedance is the driving-point impedance of a passive
    one-port, so its real part is non-negative at every frequency,

    .. math::

        \\operatorname{Re} Z(j\\,2\\pi f) \\;\\ge\\; 0 \\qquad (f \\ge 0).

    A rational fit can violate this *between* or *beyond* its samples:
    review pass 10 found a 4-pole fit of passive data (rms 4.4 mΩ, no
    warning) with :math:`\\Re Z = -0.019\\,\\Omega` at 5.5 Hz, between the
    0 Hz and 50 Hz samples (10.40 / 10.41). This is the one passivity
    check of the package: the groundinsight exporter runs the same
    implementation on the formula it writes.

    Parameters
    ----------
    fit
        :class:`VectorFitResult` or
        :class:`~groundfield.postprocess.rho_f_standard.RhoFStandardFit`.
    f_max
        Upper end of the band in Hz (the band starts at 0 Hz). Default:
        twice the highest fitted frequency, the band of the export check.
    n
        Number of points of the linear frequency grid of a vector fit
        (``>= 2``). The grid also holds ``3 n // 10`` logarithmically
        spaced points from :math:`10^{-6} f_\\max`, the samples and the
        midpoints between them, and 161 points within eight half-widths
        :math:`|\\Re p|` of every pole frequency :math:`|\\Im p|/2\\pi`,
        which resolve resonances narrower than any fixed grid. The ten
        lowest local minima of the grid are refined by a bounded scalar
        minimisation.
    rho_range
        ``(rho_min, rho_max)`` in Ω·m for a standard-form fit; default
        the sampled range. :math:`\\Re Z = k_0 + k_1\\rho + k_2 f +
        k_4 f\\rho` is bilinear, so its minimum over the box
        :math:`[\\rho_\\min, \\rho_\\max] \\times [0, f_\\max]` lies at a
        corner and the check is exact.

    Returns
    -------
    PassivityReport
        ``passed`` is ``True`` when every evaluated :math:`Z` is finite and
        :math:`\\min \\Re Z \\ge -10^{-9} \\max |Z|` (the tolerance absorbs
        round-off and the coefficient rounding of an exported formula).

    Raises
    ------
    TypeError
        For an unsupported fit type.
    ValueError
        For ``f_max <= 0``, ``n < 2`` or an invalid ``rho_range``.
    """
    return _check_passivity(fit, f_max=f_max, n=n, rho_range=rho_range)

    fit_to_sympy(fit: VectorFitResult, *, decimals: int = 6)

    Convert a VectorFitResult to a SymPy expression in s.

    The expression is the partial-fraction form of the fit,

    \[ Z(s) \;=\; R_\infty \;+\; L_\infty \cdot s \;+\; \sum_k\,\frac{r_k}{s - p_k}, \]

    with every complex-conjugate pole/residue pair combined into one real second-order term,

    \[ \frac{r}{s - p} + \frac{r^*}{s - p^*} \;=\; \frac{2\,\Re(r)\,(s - \Re(p)) - 2\,\Im(r)\,\Im(p)} {(s - \Re(p))^2 + \Im(p)^2}, \]

Each coefficient is the full-precision value correctly rounded once to decimals digits, so its relative error is at most \(\tfrac12\,10^{1-N}\) for \(N\) = decimals. Evaluated with sympy.lambdify() on reviewer R5's 98 vector fits (0 to 2 kHz), the worst deviation from VectorFitResult.evaluate(), relative to \(\max|Z|\), is \(4.0\cdot10^{-6}\) at the default 6 digits and \(4.8\cdot10^{-12}\) at 12.

    def fit_to_sympy(fit: VectorFitResult, *, decimals: int = 6):
    """Convert a :class:`VectorFitResult` to a SymPy expression in ``s``.

    The expression is the partial-fraction form of the fit,

    $$
    Z(s) \\;=\\; R_\\infty \\;+\\; L_\\infty \\cdot s \\;+\\;
    \\sum_k\\,\\frac{r_k}{s - p_k},
    $$

    with every complex-conjugate pole/residue pair combined into one
    real second-order term,

    $$
    \\frac{r}{s - p} + \\frac{r^*}{s - p^*}
    \\;=\\; \\frac{2\\,\\Re(r)\\,(s - \\Re(p)) -
                  2\\,\\Im(r)\\,\\Im(p)}
                 {(s - \\Re(p))^2 + \\Im(p)^2},
    $$

    so the expression is real for real ``s``. It is built by the renderer
    the ``groundinsight`` exporter uses (one term per real pole or pole
    pair; review pass 10, 10.73) and is not simplified: up to the
    calendar release ``sympy.simplify`` merged the terms into one rational
    function of degree four over three.

    Parameters
    ----------
    fit
        The vector fit.
    decimals
        Significant digits of every floating-point coefficient (1 to 17;
        larger values count as 17). Each coefficient is the full-precision
        value correctly rounded **once** to ``decimals`` digits, so its
        relative error is at most :math:`\\tfrac12\\,10^{1-N}` for
        :math:`N` = ``decimals``. Evaluated with :func:`sympy.lambdify`
        on reviewer R5's 98 vector fits (0 to 2 kHz), the worst deviation
        from :meth:`VectorFitResult.evaluate`, relative to
        :math:`\\max|Z|`, is :math:`4.0\\cdot10^{-6}` at the default
        6 digits and :math:`4.8\\cdot10^{-12}` at 12.

    Returns
    -------
    sympy.Expr
        Expression in the free symbol ``s`` (``sympy.Symbol("s",
        complex=True)``).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``decimals`` is not a positive integer.

    Warns
    -----
    UserWarning
        If the expression does not depend on ``s`` (a fit without poles
        and with :math:`L_\\infty = 0`).
    """
    import sympy as sp

    from groundfield.io._formula import round_coefficients

    s = sp.Symbol("s", complex=True)
    expr = round_coefficients(_partial_fractions(fit, s), decimals)

    # Defensive guard: every rho-f formula must depend on ``s``. A
    # constant Z(rho, f) silently breaks the groundinsight BusType
    # extraction, so we surface that as a ``UserWarning`` here. This
    # cannot trigger under the current ``vector_fit`` because
    # ``n_poles >= 1`` is enforced — the guard catches programmatically
    # constructed ``VectorFitResult`` objects with zero poles and zero
    # ``L_inf``.
    if s not in expr.free_symbols:
        import warnings

        warnings.warn(
            "fit_to_sympy: the resulting expression has no dependency "
            f"on the frequency-domain variable s ({expr!r}). Downstream "
            "groundinsight BusType.impedance_formula consumers expect "
            "a frequency-dependent rho-f model. Re-run vector_fit with "
            "n_poles >= 1 and at least one non-zero residue, or pass "
            "include_L_inf=True if you genuinely want a constant + "
            "inductive shoulder.",
            UserWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )

    return expr

    def rho_f_from_field_result(
    result,
    electrode_name: str | None = None,
    *,
    quantity: Quantity = "input",
    source: str | None = None,
    n_poles: int = 4,
    n_iter: int = 8,
    include_R_inf: bool = True,
    include_L_inf: bool = False,
    complex_poles: bool = True,
) -> VectorFitResult:
    """Fit $Z(s)$ to the impedance of a :class:`FieldResult`.

    Reads the impedance selected by ``quantity`` at every frequency in
    ``result.frequencies`` and runs :func:`vector_fit` on the series.

    Parameters
    ----------
    result
        :class:`groundfield.FieldResult` produced by an
        ``Engine.solve`` call with at least 4–8 frequency samples.
    electrode_name
        Electrode whose impedance is fitted. Required for
        ``quantity="cluster"`` and ``"electrode"``. With ``"input"`` it
        is optional; when given it must belong to the cluster the source
        feeds (and selects among several sources).
    quantity
        ``"input"`` (default since review pass 10, 10.19): the
        driving-point impedance :math:`(\\varphi_a - \\varphi_r)/I_s`
        of the current source (:meth:`FieldResult.input_impedance`) —
        the impedance a groundinsight BusType stands for.
        ``"cluster"``: :meth:`FieldResult.cluster_impedance` of
        ``electrode_name``. ``"electrode"``: :math:`U_e/I_e` of the
        named electrode alone, the quantity v0.15.0 fitted (17 % above
        the cluster impedance for a ring with two bonded rods).
    source
        Current source for ``quantity="input"``; may be omitted when the
        result carries exactly one.
    n_poles, n_iter, include_R_inf, include_L_inf, complex_poles
        Forwarded to :func:`vector_fit`.

    Returns
    -------
    VectorFitResult

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        For an unknown ``quantity``; for ``"input"`` on a result without
        source snapshot or with an ``electrode_name`` the source does not
        feed; for ``"cluster"`` / ``"electrode"`` without
        ``electrode_name``; if the denominator current is zero at every
        frequency.
    KeyError
        If ``electrode_name`` or ``source`` is unknown.

    Notes
    -----
    Frequencies at which the denominator current is zero (a passive
    electrode, a dead column) are masked with a :class:`UserWarning`
    instead of being entered as :math:`Z = 0`.
    """
    z_all, i_all = impedance_series(
        result,
        quantity,
        electrode_name=electrode_name,
        source=source,
        caller="rho_f_from_field_result",
    )
    freqs = np.asarray(result.frequencies, dtype=float)
    if i_all.shape != freqs.shape:
        raise ValueError(
            "Inconsistent shapes between frequencies and electrode currents"
        )
    label = f"electrode '{electrode_name}'" if quantity != "input" else "the source"
    # Audit 2026-07-08, WP-B4 (finding N23): frequencies where the
    # denominator current vanishes (passive electrode / dead column)
    # are MASKED instead of being injected as Z = 0 samples — a
    # single dead frequency used to pull the whole fit through the
    # origin silently.
    alive = np.abs(i_all) > 0.0
    if not alive.any():
        raise ValueError(
            f"rho_f_from_field_result: {label} carries no current at any "
            "frequency — Z = U/I is undefined. Fit the driven electrode "
            "instead."
        )
    if not alive.all():
        import warnings as _warnings

        _warnings.warn(
            f"rho_f_from_field_result: {label} carries no current at "
            f"{int((~alive).sum())} of {alive.size} frequencies; those "
            "samples are excluded from the fit (historic behaviour injected "
            "Z = 0 there).",
            UserWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )
    fit = vector_fit(
        freqs[alive],
        z_all[alive],
        n_poles=n_poles,
        n_iter=n_iter,
        include_R_inf=include_R_inf,
        include_L_inf=include_L_inf,
        complex_poles=complex_poles,
    )
    return dataclasses.replace(fit, quantity=quantity)

    vector_fit ¶

    vector_fit(frequencies: Sequence[float], Z_values: Sequence[complex], *, n_poles: int = 4, n_iter: int = 8, include_R_inf: bool = True, include_L_inf: bool = False, complex_poles: bool = True, weighting: str = 'uniform', rms_tol: float = 0.01) -> VectorFitResult

    Fit a rational \(Z(s)\) approximation to a sampled frequency response.

    Implements the Vector Fitting algorithm of Gustavsen & Semlyen 1999 in its single-output, equal-weight form. The denominator polynomial is shared between numerator and denominator estimation (Sanathanan-Koerner with iterative pole relocation); after n_iter outer iterations the poles are taken as fixed and the residues are solved from a final linear system.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    frequencies Sequence[float]

    Frequency samples in Hz, length \(N\).

    		 required
    Z_values Sequence[complex]

    Complex impedance samples \(Z(j2\pi f_k)\) in \(\Omega\), length \(N\).

    		 required
    n_poles int

    Target number of poles. Complex-conjugate pairs count as 2 poles each.

    		 4
    n_iter int

    Number of pole-relocation iterations.

    		 8
    include_R_inf bool

    Whether to fit a constant offset \(R_\infty\) (DC residual).

    		 True
    include_L_inf bool

    Whether to fit a \(s\cdot L_\infty\) proportional term.

    		 False
    complex_poles bool

    True (default) initialises with complex-conjugate pole pairs, suitable for resonant behaviour. Set False for purely-resistive / monotonic responses.

    		 True
    weighting str

    "uniform" (default, historic behaviour) or "inverse_magnitude": weights every sample by 1/|Z_n|, the standard remedy when |Z| spans several decades and the unweighted LS would fit only the largest magnitudes (audit 2026-07-08, WP-B4).

    		 'uniform'
    rms_tol float

    Warn with VectorFitQualityWarning when the relative rms error rms_error / mean|Z| exceeds this value (default 0.01).

    		 0.01

    Raises:

    Type Description
    ValueError

    If the samples are not finite, no sample has f > 0, n_poles < 1, weighting is unknown, or the least-squares problem cannot be solved (instead of numpy's LinAlgError).

    Warns:

    Type Description
    VectorFitQualityWarning

    Relative rms above rms_tol; imaginary part of a 0 Hz sample above 0.1 % of its magnitude (discarded).
    (VectorFitConvergenceWarning, VectorFitUnderdeterminedWarning)

    See the warning classes.
    Notes

    0 Hz samples (review pass 10, 10.41). The model has real coefficients, so it is real at \(s = 0\). A 0 Hz sample with an imaginary part (measured or averaged data) cannot be represented; up to v0.15.0 the pole relocation then moved a pole onto the origin and the fit collapsed to \(Z \approx 0\) at every other frequency (relative rms 0.99, 20 of 20 noisy data sets) or numpy raised LinAlgError. The 0 Hz samples are now projected onto their real part before fitting, which is bit-for-bit neutral for real 0 Hz samples (all solver output).

    Since the 2026-07-08 audit (WP-B4) the least-squares systems use the conjugate-pair real basis (see _pair_basis()): complex pole pairs carry genuinely complex residues, matching the cited Gustavsen & Semlyen algorithm. The pole-relocation loop additionally monitors the relative pole displacement, breaks early below 1e-8 and warns (VectorFitConvergenceWarning) when it is still above 1 % after n_iter iterations; the diagnostics are exposed as VectorFitResult.n_iter_used / pole_shift.

    Returns:

    Type Description
    VectorFitResult

    frequencies: Sequence[float],
    Z_values: Sequence[complex],
    *,
    n_poles: int = 4,
    n_iter: int = 8,
    include_R_inf: bool = True,
    include_L_inf: bool = False,
    complex_poles: bool = True,
    weighting: str = "uniform",
    rms_tol: float = 0.01,
) -> VectorFitResult:
    """Fit a rational $Z(s)$ approximation to a sampled frequency response.

    Implements the Vector Fitting algorithm of Gustavsen & Semlyen
    1999 in its single-output, equal-weight form. The denominator
    polynomial is shared between numerator and denominator
    estimation (Sanathanan-Koerner with iterative pole relocation);
    after ``n_iter`` outer iterations the poles are taken as fixed
    and the residues are solved from a final linear system.

    Parameters
    ----------
    frequencies
        Frequency samples in Hz, length $N$.
    Z_values
        Complex impedance samples $Z(j2\\pi f_k)$ in $\\Omega$,
        length $N$.
    n_poles
        Target number of poles. Complex-conjugate pairs count as
        2 poles each.
    n_iter
        Number of pole-relocation iterations.
    include_R_inf
        Whether to fit a constant offset $R_\\infty$ (DC residual).
    include_L_inf
        Whether to fit a $s\\cdot L_\\infty$ proportional term.
    complex_poles
        ``True`` (default) initialises with complex-conjugate pole
        pairs, suitable for resonant behaviour. Set ``False`` for
        purely-resistive / monotonic responses.
    weighting
        ``"uniform"`` (default, historic behaviour) or
        ``"inverse_magnitude"``: weights every sample by
        ``1/|Z_n|``, the standard remedy when ``|Z|`` spans several
        decades and the unweighted LS would fit only the largest
        magnitudes (audit 2026-07-08, WP-B4).
    rms_tol
        Warn with :class:`VectorFitQualityWarning` when the relative rms
        error ``rms_error / mean|Z|`` exceeds this value (default 0.01).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the samples are not finite, no sample has ``f > 0``,
        ``n_poles < 1``, ``weighting`` is unknown, or the least-squares
        problem cannot be solved (instead of numpy's ``LinAlgError``).

    Warns
    -----
    VectorFitQualityWarning
        Relative rms above ``rms_tol``; imaginary part of a 0 Hz sample
        above 0.1 % of its magnitude (discarded).
    VectorFitConvergenceWarning, VectorFitUnderdeterminedWarning
        See the warning classes.

    Notes
    -----
    **0 Hz samples** (review pass 10, 10.41). The model has real
    coefficients, so it is real at :math:`s = 0`. A 0 Hz sample with an
    imaginary part (measured or averaged data) cannot be represented;
    up to v0.15.0 the pole relocation then moved a pole onto the origin
    and the fit collapsed to :math:`Z \\approx 0` at every other
    frequency (relative rms 0.99, 20 of 20 noisy data sets) or numpy
    raised ``LinAlgError``. The 0 Hz samples are now projected onto
    their real part before fitting, which is bit-for-bit neutral for
    real 0 Hz samples (all solver output).

    Since the 2026-07-08 audit (WP-B4) the least-squares systems use
    the **conjugate-pair real basis** (see :func:`_pair_basis`):
    complex pole pairs carry genuinely complex residues, matching
    the cited Gustavsen & Semlyen algorithm. The pole-relocation
    loop additionally monitors the relative pole displacement,
    breaks early below ``1e-8`` and warns
    (:class:`VectorFitConvergenceWarning`) when it is still above
    1 % after ``n_iter`` iterations; the diagnostics are exposed as
    ``VectorFitResult.n_iter_used`` / ``pole_shift``.

    Returns
    -------
    VectorFitResult
    """
    frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float)
    Z = np.asarray(Z_values, dtype=complex)
    if frequencies.shape != Z.shape:
        raise ValueError("frequencies and Z_values must have the same shape")
    if not (np.all(np.isfinite(frequencies)) and np.all(np.isfinite(Z))):
        raise ValueError("vector_fit: frequencies and Z_values must be finite.")
    if not np.any(frequencies > 0.0):
        raise ValueError(
            "vector_fit: needs at least one sample with f > 0; a pure DC "
            "data set has no frequency dependence to fit."
        )
    dc = frequencies == 0.0
    if np.any(dc) and np.any(Z[dc].imag != 0.0):
        # A real-coefficient rational model is real at s = 0: project
        # the 0 Hz samples onto their real part (10.41). Bit-neutral for
        # real DC samples.
        worst = float(np.max(np.abs(Z[dc].imag) / np.maximum(np.abs(Z[dc]), 1e-300)))
        if worst > 1e-3:
            import warnings as _warnings

            _warnings.warn(
                "vector_fit: the 0 Hz sample has an imaginary part of "
                f"{worst:.2%} of its magnitude; it is discarded (the rational "
                "model is real at f = 0). Check the DC value of the data.",
                VectorFitQualityWarning,
                stacklevel=2,
            )
        Z = Z.copy()
        Z[dc] = Z[dc].real
    if n_poles < 1:
        raise ValueError(
            "vector_fit: n_poles must be at least 1, got "
            f"n_poles={n_poles}. n_poles == 0 produces an s-free fit "
            "whose SymPy conversion yields a constant Z(rho, f) "
            "expression without frequency dependence — that is never "
            "the intended behaviour, so this case is rejected at the "
            "API boundary."
        )
    # The previous trigger
    # ``2 * n_poles >= N`` counted 4 real DOFs per pole regardless of
    # whether the search was constrained to conjugate-symmetric pairs.
    # Under ``complex_poles=True`` (the default) the conjugate-symmetry
    # constraint halves the actual free parameters: a pair carries
    # 4 real DOFs (real pole, imag pole, real residue, imag residue),
    # and a lone unpaired real pole carries 2. The corrected formula
    # counts ``n_independent_poles = n_poles // 2 + (n_poles % 2)`` for
    # the pair-constrained search and ``n_poles`` for the all-real one.
    # The strict ``>`` in the conjugate branch keeps a uniquely
    # determined fit (e.g. ``n_poles=2, N=2``) from emitting a false
    # positive.
    if complex_poles:
        n_independent_poles = n_poles // 2 + (n_poles % 2)
        is_underdetermined = 2 * n_independent_poles > frequencies.size
    else:
        is_underdetermined = 2 * n_poles >= frequencies.size
    if is_underdetermined:
        import warnings as _warnings

        if complex_poles:
            ratio_explanation = (
                "2 * n_independent_poles > len(frequencies) is the "
                "critical ratio under complex-conjugate-pair fitting"
            )
        else:
            ratio_explanation = (
                "2 * n_poles >= len(frequencies) is the critical "
                "ratio under all-real-pole fitting"
            )
        _warnings.warn(
            "vector_fit: n_poles="
            f"{n_poles} with len(frequencies)={frequencies.size} "
            "leads to an under- or exactly-determined least-squares "
            "fit (each pole contributes residue + pole-location "
            f"DOFs; {ratio_explanation}). The numerical solve may "
            "succeed but produces an identity interpolation of the "
            "input samples that carries no information beyond the "
            "raw frequency response. Reduce n_poles to "
            f"{max(1, frequencies.size // 2 - 1)} or fewer, or supply "
            "more frequency samples.",
            VectorFitUnderdeterminedWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )
    if weighting not in ("uniform", "inverse_magnitude"):
        raise ValueError(
            "vector_fit: weighting must be 'uniform' or "
            f"'inverse_magnitude', got {weighting!r}."
        )
    s = 2j * math.pi * frequencies
    if weighting == "inverse_magnitude":
        w = 1.0 / np.maximum(np.abs(Z), 1e-12 * float(np.max(np.abs(Z))))
    else:
        w = np.ones(s.size)

    poles = _initial_poles(frequencies, n_poles, complex_conj=complex_poles)
    poles = _enforce_conjugate_symmetry(poles)

    # Outer loop: pole relocation. The system is, schematically,
    #   sum_k r_k / (s_n - p_k) + d + s_n*h - sum_k r'_k Z_n / (s_n - p_k)
    #     = Z_n
    # where {r_k, d, h, r'_k} are the unknowns and the new poles are
    # the zeros of the denominator polynomial 1 + sum r'_k/(s-p_k).
    # Both the numerator residues r_k and the sigma residues r'_k use
    # the conjugate-pair real basis (audit 2026-07-08, WP-B4), so
    # complex pole pairs carry genuinely complex residues.
    extras = (1 if include_R_inf else 0) + (1 if include_L_inf else 0)
    n_iter_used = 0
    pole_shift = float("inf")
    for _ in range(max(1, n_iter)):
        structure = _pole_pair_structure(poles)
        basis = _pair_basis(s, poles, structure)  # (N, n_poles)
        A = np.zeros((s.size, n_poles + extras + n_poles), dtype=complex)
        A[:, :n_poles] = basis
        col = n_poles
        if include_R_inf:
            A[:, col] = 1.0
            col += 1
        if include_L_inf:
            A[:, col] = s
            col += 1
        A[:, col : col + n_poles] = -Z[:, None] * basis

        # Solve with real-imag stacking (least-squares), optionally
        # row-weighted.
        Aw = A * w[:, None]
        M = np.vstack([Aw.real, Aw.imag])
        rhs = np.concatenate([(w * Z).real, (w * Z).imag])
        sol = _solve_lstsq(M, rhs, poles)

        # Reconstruct the complex sigma residues from the pair basis.
        sigma_residues = _coeffs_to_residues(
            sol[n_poles + extras :],
            poles,
            structure,
        )
        # New poles: eigenvalues of A_p - b·c^T where A_p = diag(poles),
        # b = ones, c = sigma_residues. (Standard Gustavsen formulation.)
        Ap = np.diag(poles)
        b = np.ones(n_poles)
        try:
            new_poles = np.linalg.eigvals(Ap - np.outer(b, sigma_residues))
        except np.linalg.LinAlgError as exc:
            raise ValueError(
                f"vector_fit: pole relocation failed ({exc}); reduce n_poles or "
                "check the samples."
            ) from exc
        new_poles = _enforce_stability(new_poles)
        new_poles = _enforce_conjugate_symmetry(new_poles)
        # Sort for deterministic order (deepest |imag| first).
        sorted_idx = np.argsort(-np.abs(new_poles.imag))
        new_poles = new_poles[sorted_idx]
        n_iter_used += 1
        scale = float(np.max(np.abs(poles))) or 1.0
        pole_shift = (
            float(np.max(np.abs(np.sort_complex(new_poles) - np.sort_complex(poles))))
            / scale
        )
        poles = new_poles
        if pole_shift < 1e-8:
            break
    if pole_shift > 1e-2:
        import warnings as _warnings

        _warnings.warn(
            f"vector_fit: pole relocation did not converge within "
            f"n_iter={n_iter} iterations (last relative pole shift "
            f"{pole_shift:.2e}). The returned fit may sit in a limit "
            "cycle; inspect rms_error, increase n_iter, or adjust "
            "n_poles / weighting.",
            VectorFitConvergenceWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )

    # Final residue solve with the converged poles (pair basis —
    # residues at conjugate poles are exact conjugates by
    # construction, no post-hoc repair required).
    structure = _pole_pair_structure(poles)
    basis = _pair_basis(s, poles, structure)
    A = np.zeros((s.size, n_poles + extras), dtype=complex)
    A[:, :n_poles] = basis
    col = n_poles
    if include_R_inf:
        A[:, col] = 1.0
        col += 1
    if include_L_inf:
        A[:, col] = s
        col += 1
    Aw = A * w[:, None]
    M = np.vstack([Aw.real, Aw.imag])
    rhs = np.concatenate([(w * Z).real, (w * Z).imag])
    sol = _solve_lstsq(M, rhs, poles)
    residues = _coeffs_to_residues(sol[:n_poles], poles, structure)
    R_inf = float(sol[n_poles]) if include_R_inf else 0.0
    L_inf = float(sol[n_poles + (1 if include_R_inf else 0)]) if include_L_inf else 0.0

    Z_fit = (
        np.full_like(s, R_inf, dtype=complex)
        + L_inf * s
        + np.sum(residues[:, None] / (s[None, :] - poles[:, None]), axis=0)
    )
    rms = float(np.sqrt(np.mean(np.abs(Z_fit - Z) ** 2)))
    rms_rel = rms / max(float(np.mean(np.abs(Z))), 1e-300)
    if rms_rel > rms_tol:
        import warnings as _warnings

        _warnings.warn(
            f"vector_fit: relative rms error {rms_rel:.2%} exceeds "
            f"{rms_tol:.2%} (n_poles={n_poles}). The rational model does not "
            "represent the samples; try another n_poles, more samples or "
            "weighting='inverse_magnitude'.",
            VectorFitQualityWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )

    return VectorFitResult(
        rms_relative=rms_rel,
        n_iter_used=n_iter_used,
        pole_shift=pole_shift,
        poles=poles,
        residues=residues,
        R_inf=R_inf,
        L_inf=L_inf,
        rms_error=rms,
        fit_frequencies=frequencies,
        fit_values=Z,
    )

    Standard rho-f form¶

    rho_f_standard ¶

    Standard-form rho-f model for the groundinsight bridge.

    The reduced grounding-cluster impedance uses the physically-motivated standard form

    \[ Z(\rho, f) \;=\; k_0 \;+\; k_1 \rho \;+\; (k_2 + j k_3)\,f \;+\; (k_4 + j k_5)\,f\,\rho, \]

    with \(\rho\) a soil-resistivity parameter (typically the upper-layer \(\rho_1\) in a fixed-structure 2-layer setup) and \(f\) the frequency. The real coefficients have direct physical interpretation:

    • \(k_0\) — resistance that does not scale with \(\rho\) in \(\Omega\): the share of the lower layer in a \(\rho_1\) sweep (\(R(\rho_1 \to 0)\) stays finite, set by \(\rho_2\)), or the series resistance of conductors in a network. Optional (k0=True by default since review pass 10, 10.27); real, so that \(Z(f = 0)\) is real.
    • \(k_1\,\rho\) — DC spreading resistance (Dwight-class scaling with the dominant local soil resistivity).
    • \(k_2\,f\) — soil-independent resistive frequency dependence in \(\Omega/\mathrm{Hz}\) (skin/proximity losses of the metallic parts; negligible in most quasi-static typical studies).
    • \(k_3\,f\) — soil-independent reactive coupling in \(\Omega/\mathrm{Hz}\), i.e. the loop-inductance term of a metallic path; the equivalent inductance is \(L = k_3 / (2\pi)\) in H.
    • \(k_4\,f\,\rho\) — Carson-type earth-return resistance: scales with both frequency and soil resistivity.
    • \(k_5\,f\,\rho\) — Carson-type earth-return reactance.

    This is not a general rational function — it is a fixed parametric ansatz that captures the leading orders for production-grade grounding-cluster impedances. It is fitted from a parametric family of groundfield runs that span both \(\rho\) and \(f\), and exported as a SymPy expression with two free symbols \(\rho\) (rho) and \(f\) (f) — the BusType.impedance_formula convention used by groundinsight.

    Mathematically the fit is a weighted linear least-squares problem:

    • Real part: \(\Re Z = k_0 + k_1\rho + k_2 f + k_4 f\rho\) → regression in (\(1\), \(\rho\), \(f\), \(f\rho\)).
    • Imaginary part: \(\Im Z = k_3 f + k_5 f\rho\) → regression in (\(f\), \(f\rho\)).

    With weights="relative" (default since review pass 10) every sample is weighted by \(1/|Z_n|\), i.e. the fit minimises the sum of squared relative errors; with "uniform" it minimises absolute errors, which concentrates the error on the low-impedance samples (low \(\rho\)), where the high-\(\rho\) samples dominate the residual.

    So \(k_2\) and \(k_4\) live in the real (resistive) half and \(k_3\) and \(k_5\) in the imaginary (reactive) half — the pairing implied by the complex factors \((k_2 + j k_3)\) and \((k_4 + j k_5)\) above.

    Both halves are decoupled in the coefficients, so the fit is unique whenever the sample set spans at least two distinct \(\rho\) values and at least two distinct frequencies (and, with \(k_0\), the real design matrix has full rank). The two conditions remove two different collinearities of the design matrix:

    • A single \(\rho = R\) makes the columns \(f\) and \(f\rho = R f\) proportional, so only \(k_2 + R\,k_4\) (resp. \(k_3 + R\,k_5\)) is identifiable.
    • A single \(f = F\) makes the columns \(\rho\) and \(f\rho = F\rho\) proportional, so only \(k_1 + F\,k_4\) is identifiable.
    Fit quality

    rms_relative (rms error over the mean \(|Z|\)) is dominated by the high-impedance samples and hides large relative errors at low \(\rho\). max_relative = \(\max_n |Z_\text{fit} - Z_n| / |Z_n|\) is the figure to check; above max_relative_tol (5 %) the fit warns with RhoFStandardQualityWarning. Review pass 10 measured on a \(\rho_1\) sweep (30…1000 Ω·m) of a 2 m ring in two-layer soil (\(\rho_2\) = 100 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m): v0.15.0 form 27 % worst error at \(\rho_1\) = 30 (rms_relative 2.6 %), with \(k_0\) and relative weights 3.3 %; an AP1-like station (4 m × 4 m loop with three 4 m rods) 43 % against 6.2 %.

    References
    • The rho-f model is the reduced grey-box representation handed to groundinsight.
    • groundinsight.BusType.impedance_formula: the consumer of the SymPy expression returned by fit_to_sympy_standard().

    def evaluate(
    self,
    rho: float | np.ndarray,
    f: float | np.ndarray,
) -> complex | np.ndarray:
    """Evaluate the fitted $Z(\\rho, f)$ in Ω at arbitrary points.

    Parameters
    ----------
    rho
        Soil resistivity in Ω·m (scalar or array).
    f
        Frequency in Hz (scalar or array, broadcast with ``rho``).
    """
    rho = np.asarray(rho, dtype=float)
    f = np.asarray(f, dtype=float)
    return (
        self.k0
        + self.k1 * rho
        + (self.k2 + 1j * self.k3) * f
        + (self.k4 + 1j * self.k5) * f * rho
    )

    RhoFStandardQualityWarning ¶

    Bases: UserWarning

    The standard-form fit misses a sample by more than max_relative_tol.

    The standard form is a fixed ansatz; a large pointwise error means it cannot represent the sampled \(Z(\rho, f)\) (review pass 10, 10.27). Check RhoFStandardFit.max_relative, restrict the \(\rho\) range, or fit per \(\rho\) with vector fitting.

    def fit_rho_f_standard(
    rho_samples: Sequence[float],
    f_samples: Sequence[float],
    Z_samples: Sequence[complex],
    *,
    k0: bool = True,
    weights: Weights = "relative",
    max_relative_tol: float = 0.05,
) -> RhoFStandardFit:
    """Fit the standard rho-f form via weighted linear least squares.

    Parameters
    ----------
    rho_samples
        Soil-resistivity values $\\rho$ in $\\Omega\\,\\mathrm{m}$
        for each sample (length $N$).
    f_samples
        Frequencies $f$ in Hz for each sample (length $N$).
    Z_samples
        Complex impedances $Z$ in $\\Omega$ at each $(\\rho, f)$ sample
        (length $N$).
    k0
        Fit the constant term $k_0$ (default ``True`` since review pass
        10, 10.27). ``False`` gives the five-coefficient form of v0.15.0.
    weights
        ``"relative"`` (default since review pass 10): weight each
        sample by $1/|Z_n|$ — minimise relative errors. ``"uniform"``:
        minimise absolute errors (v0.15.0).
    max_relative_tol
        Warn with :class:`RhoFStandardQualityWarning` when
        ``max_relative`` exceeds this value (dimensionless, default
        0.05).

    Returns
    -------
    RhoFStandardFit

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If sample arrays have inconsistent lengths, there are fewer than
        four samples, fewer than two distinct $\\rho$ values *or* fewer
        than two distinct $f$ values, the design matrix is rank
        deficient, ``weights`` is unknown, or ``weights="relative"`` meets
        a sample with $Z = 0$.

    Warns
    -----
    RhoFStandardQualityWarning
        If the worst pointwise relative error exceeds ``max_relative_tol``.

    Notes
    -----
    ``k0=False, weights="uniform"`` reproduces the v0.15.0 coefficients
    bit for bit.
    """
    rho = np.asarray(rho_samples, dtype=float)
    f = np.asarray(f_samples, dtype=float)
    Z = np.asarray(Z_samples, dtype=complex)
    if rho.shape != f.shape or rho.shape != Z.shape:
        raise ValueError(
            "rho_samples, f_samples and Z_samples must have identical shape; "
            f"got rho={rho.shape}, f={f.shape}, Z={Z.shape}."
        )
    if rho.size < 4:
        raise ValueError(
            f"fit_rho_f_standard needs at least 4 samples; got {rho.size}."
        )
    # Identifiability: a constant rho makes the columns f and f*rho
    # proportional (k2/k4 and k3/k5 confounded); a constant f makes
    # the columns rho and f*rho proportional (k1/k4 confounded).
    if np.unique(rho).size < 2:
        raise ValueError(
            "fit_rho_f_standard needs at least two distinct rho values "
            "to identify k2 and k4 (and k3 and k5) separately."
        )
    if np.unique(f).size < 2:
        raise ValueError(
            "fit_rho_f_standard needs at least two distinct f values "
            "to identify k1 and k4 separately."
        )
    if weights not in ("uniform", "relative"):
        raise ValueError(f"weights must be 'uniform' or 'relative', got {weights!r}.")
    absZ = np.abs(Z)
    if weights == "relative":
        if np.any(absZ == 0.0):
            raise ValueError(
                "weights='relative' needs |Z| > 0 at every sample; use "
                "weights='uniform' or drop the zero samples."
            )
        w = 1.0 / absZ
    else:
        w = None

    # Real part: Re(Z) = k0 + k1·ρ + k2·f + k4·f·ρ
    cols = [rho, f, f * rho]
    if k0:
        cols.insert(0, np.ones_like(rho))
    A_real = np.column_stack(cols)
    A_imag = np.column_stack([f, f * rho])
    b_real, b_imag = Z.real, Z.imag
    if w is not None:
        A_real, b_real = A_real * w[:, None], b_real * w
        A_imag, b_imag = A_imag * w[:, None], b_imag * w
    sol_real = _lstsq(A_real, b_real, "real-part")
    c0 = float(sol_real[0]) if k0 else 0.0
    k1, k2, k4 = (float(x) for x in sol_real[-3:])

    # Imag part: Im(Z) = k3·f + k5·f·ρ
    sol_imag = _lstsq(A_imag, b_imag, "imaginary-part")
    k3, k5 = float(sol_imag[0]), float(sol_imag[1])

    Z_fit = c0 + k1 * rho + (k2 + 1j * k3) * f + (k4 + 1j * k5) * f * rho
    err = np.abs(Z_fit - Z)
    rms = float(np.sqrt(np.mean(err**2)))
    rms_rel = rms / max(float(np.mean(absZ)), 1e-12)
    nonzero = absZ > 0.0
    max_rel = float(np.max(err[nonzero] / absZ[nonzero])) if nonzero.any() else math.nan
    if max_rel > max_relative_tol:
        worst = int(np.flatnonzero(nonzero)[np.argmax(err[nonzero] / absZ[nonzero])])
        warnings.warn(
            f"fit_rho_f_standard: max_relative = {max_rel:.1%} exceeds "
            f"{max_relative_tol:.1%} (worst sample rho = {rho[worst]:g} Ohm m, "
            f"f = {f[worst]:g} Hz; rms_relative = {rms_rel:.1%}). The standard "
            "form does not represent these samples well.",
            RhoFStandardQualityWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )

    return RhoFStandardFit(
        k1=k1,
        k2=k2,
        k3=k3,
        k4=k4,
        k5=k5,
        rms_error=rms,
        rms_relative=rms_rel,
        sample_rho=rho,
        sample_f=f,
        sample_Z=Z,
        k0=c0,
        max_relative=max_rel,
        weights=weights,
    )

    def fit_to_sympy_standard(fit: RhoFStandardFit, *, decimals: int = 6):
    """Convert a :class:`RhoFStandardFit` to a SymPy expression.

    Returns a :class:`sympy.Expr` in two free symbols ``rho`` and
    ``f`` (both real), in the standard form

    $$
    Z(\\rho, f) \\;=\\; k_0 \\;+\\; k_1\\rho \\;+\\; (k_2 + j k_3)\\,f
                      \\;+\\; (k_4 + j k_5)\\,f\\,\\rho,
    $$

    the constant term only when it is non-zero. The expression is built
    term by term by the renderer the ``groundinsight`` exporter uses
    (review pass 10, 10.73) and is suitable for direct insertion into
    ``groundinsight.BusType.impedance_formula``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    fit
        Standard-form fit.
    decimals
        Significant digits of every coefficient (1 to 17; larger values
        count as 17). Each coefficient is correctly rounded **once**, so
        its relative error is at most :math:`\\tfrac12\\,10^{1-N}` for
        :math:`N` = ``decimals``.

    Returns
    -------
    sympy.Expr

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``decimals`` is not a positive integer.
    """
    import sympy as sp

    from groundfield.io._formula import round_coefficients

    rho = sp.Symbol("rho", real=True, positive=True)
    f = sp.Symbol("f", real=True, positive=True)
    return round_coefficients(_standard_expression(fit, rho, f), decimals)
